title: Projects
text:
Quantitative finance

A parallel Monte Carlo framework in C
An object-oriented Monte Carlo framework for derivative pricing, designed to reuse stochastic processes and product definitions and distribute simulations across parallel workers. The original project proposed a European option comparison and applications to path-dependent products. The accompanying note and source files are not included in this archive.


Bootstrapping a SOFR curve
A QuantLib exploration of constructing an overnight-indexed swap curve and repricing its calibration instruments.
Read the SOFR curve note.

title: Projects
text:
Physics

Self-consistent calculations in silicon nanostructures
An iterative calculation of electron eigenfunctions and energies in a silicon inversion layer, developed in collaboration with Dr G. Gopir. The work coupled electrostatic and quantum calculations and explored adaptive boundary conditions to improve convergence. The previous website records publication in Solid State Science and Technology, 20, 88–95.



Convergence of the self-consistent calculation.




Controlling the repulsive Casimir force
Theoretical work with Prof C. H. Raymond Ooi on varying the Casimir force between parallel plates through the optical Kerr effect. The calculations explored how changing incident laser intensity could change the force between attraction and repulsion for suitable materials.
The work appeared in Physical Review A, 86, 062509 and Sains Malaysiana, 42(12), 1799–1803. The original code is in the Casimir force repository.



Casimir force as a function of separation.

title: European Call Greeks: A Visual Risk Map
text:
Where does option risk actually live across spot and maturity?
The Black–Scholes formulas answer the pointwise question, but the location and concentration of risk are much easier to see in curves. I use a plain European call as a controlled case: a non-dividend-paying stock with \(K=100\), \(r=3\%\), and \(\sigma=20\%\). The focus is not the formulas themselves, but how quickly the risk profile changes as expiry approaches.

title: European Call Greeks: A Visual Risk Map
text:
Reference setup
The call value is
\[
C(S,K,T,r,\sigma)=S N(d_1)-K e^{-rT}N(d_2),
\]
where
\[
\begin{aligned}
d_1&=\frac{\ln(S/K)+(r+\tfrac12\sigma^2)T}{\sigma\sqrt{T}},\\
d_2&=d_1-\sigma\sqrt{T}.
\end{aligned}
\]
All plots use the same \(S\in[50,150]\) grid and mark \(S=K\). I use 1,001 spot points because a coarse grid can make the one-week gamma profile look materially less concentrated than it is.

title: European Call Greeks: A Visual Risk Map
text:
Start with the value curve


Show Python
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(spots, np.maximum(spots - K, 0.0), color="0.15", linestyle=":", linewidth=2.0, label="Payoff")
for label, maturity in maturities.items():
    ax.plot(
        spots,
        call_price(spots, K, maturity, r, sigma),
        label=label,
        color=maturity_colors[label],
        linewidth=1.8,
    )
finish_spot_axis(ax, "Call value")
ax.legend(ncol=3, frameon=False)
plt.show()








Figure 1: Call value approaches the terminal payoff as maturity contracts.





The feature I would pay attention to is the width of the transition around the strike. It contracts sharply with maturity. The Greeks below are different views of that narrowing region.

title: European Call Greeks: A Visual Risk Map
text:
Delta: the transition region


Show Python
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
plot_across_maturities(ax, call_delta, "Delta")
ax.set_ylim(-0.03, 1.03)
plt.show()








Figure 2: Call delta transitions from zero to one across the exercise boundary.





For reference, \(\Delta=N(d_1)\). The levels near zero and one are not the interesting part of this chart. The useful information is where delta changes rapidly, and how narrow that region becomes near expiry. That is where a small spot move changes the hedge materially.
The transition is not centred mechanically on the cash strike. Rates, carry, volatility, and maturity enter through \(d_1\); even in this simple case, spot ATM does not imply a delta of exactly \(0.5\).

title: European Call Greeks: A Visual Risk Map
text:
Gamma: concentration near expiry


Show Python
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
plot_across_maturities(ax, call_gamma, "Gamma")
plt.show()








Figure 3: Short maturity concentrates gamma near the strike.





The analytic reference is
\[
\Gamma=\frac{\partial^2 C}{\partial S^2}
=\frac{\phi(d_1)}{S\sigma\sqrt{T}}.
\]
What I find useful here is how quickly gamma stops being a broad exposure and becomes a local one. At one week, most of the curvature sits in a narrow band near the strike. A position can cross that band in an ordinary spot move, so a hedge inferred from one point can age badly before the next rebalance.
This is also the first validation warning. The formula is smooth, but a grid or finite-difference bump that is wide relative to the peak will average over the very feature being measured.

title: European Call Greeks: A Visual Risk Map
section: Vega: similar location, different maturity behaviour
text:
Vega: similar location, different maturity behaviour
The chart reports vega per one volatility point, i.e. \(\mathcal{V}/100\).


Show Python
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
plot_across_maturities(ax, lambda S, K, T, r, vol: call_vega(S, K, T, r, vol) / 100.0, "Vega per 1 vol point")
plt.show()








Figure 4: Vega is largest where the exercise outcome remains uncertain.





Per unit change in volatility,
\[
\mathcal{V}=\frac{\partial C}{\partial\sigma}
=S\phi(d_1)\sqrt{T}.
\]
Vega occupies roughly the same decision region as gamma, but maturity pushes the two exposures in opposite directions. Near expiry, gamma becomes taller and narrower while vega collapses because there is little time left for additional dispersion. Treating both as generic measures of “optionality” hides a useful distinction: gamma is becoming more acute precisely as vega is disappearing.

title: European Call Greeks: A Visual Risk Map
text:
Theta: read it with gamma
The chart scales annual calendar theta to a daily amount using \(\Theta/365\).


Show Python
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
plot_across_maturities(ax, lambda S, K, T, r, vol: call_theta(S, K, T, r, vol) / 365.0, "Theta per calendar day")
plt.show()








Figure 5: Daily theta becomes sharply negative around ATM near expiry.





Annual calendar theta is
\[
\Theta=-\frac{S\phi(d_1)\sigma}{2\sqrt{T}}
-rKe^{-rT}N(d_2).
\]
I would not read this plot independently of gamma. The sharp negative pocket near the strike is the carry cost attached to the same local curvature seen above. In the Black–Scholes PDE,
\[
\Theta+\frac12\sigma^2S^2\Gamma+rS\Delta-rV=0,
\]
the diffusion term associated with positive gamma is offset by theta and carry. The co-location matters more than either headline Greek: the position earns or loses most of its gamma/theta economics inside a shrinking spot interval.

title: European Call Greeks: A Visual Risk Map
text:
How volatility redistributes risk
Fix \(T=1\) year and vary \(\sigma\). The issue is not only how much the option is worth, but where its risk sits across spot.


Show Python
volatilities = {"10%": 0.10, "20%": 0.20, "40%": 0.40, "60%": 0.60}
vol_colors = dict(zip(volatilities, plt.cm.cividis(np.linspace(0.08, 0.9, len(volatilities)))))
panels = [
    (call_price, "Call value", "PV"),
    (call_delta, "Delta", "Delta"),
    (call_gamma, "Gamma", "Gamma"),
]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, sharex=True, figsize=(8, 10))
for ax, (measure, ylabel, title) in zip(axes, panels):
    for label, vol in volatilities.items():
        ax.plot(
            spots,
            measure(spots, K, 1.0, r, vol),
            label=label,
            color=vol_colors[label],
            linewidth=1.8,
        )
    finish_spot_axis(ax, ylabel, xlabel=ax is axes[-1])
    ax.set_title(title, loc="left")

axes[0].legend(ncol=4, frameon=False, title="Volatility")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 6: Higher volatility raises value and distributes the delta transition and gamma over a wider spot region.





Higher volatility broadens the delta transition and distributes gamma across a wider spot range. At low volatility, the risk is more concentrated. Cash gamma contains a \(1/S\) scaling, so the peak need not sit exactly at the strike; in this setup it moves lower in spot as volatility rises. The practical point is that volatility changes where hedge risk sits, not only the option PV.

title: European Call Greeks: A Visual Risk Map
text:
Numerical verification
Analytic formulas are reference values, not independent evidence that an implementation is correct. The table compares analytic delta, gamma, and vega with central differences at \(S\in\{80,100,120\}\), using \(T=1\), a spot bump of \(0.10\), and an absolute volatility bump of \(10^{-4}\) (one volatility basis point).


Show Python
rows = []
for spot in (80.0, 100.0, 120.0):
    analytic = {
        "Delta": float(call_delta(spot, K, 1.0, r, sigma)),
        "Gamma": float(call_gamma(spot, K, 1.0, r, sigma)),
        "Vega": float(call_vega(spot, K, 1.0, r, sigma)),
    }
    finite_difference = finite_difference_greeks(
        spot,
        K,
        1.0,
        r,
        sigma,
        spot_bump=0.10,
        volatility_bump=1.0e-4,
    )
    for greek, key in (("Delta", "delta"), ("Gamma", "gamma"), ("Vega", "vega")):
        estimate = float(finite_difference[key])
        rows.append((spot, greek, analytic[greek], estimate, abs(analytic[greek] - estimate)))

assert max(row[4] for row in rows if row[1] == "Delta") < 2.0e-6
assert max(row[4] for row in rows if row[1] == "Gamma") < 1.0e-7
assert max(row[4] for row in rows if row[1] == "Vega") < 1.0e-5

table = [
    "| Spot | Greek | Analytic | Central difference | Absolute error |",
    "|---:|:---|---:|---:|---:|",
]
table.extend(
    f"| {spot:.0f} | {greek} | {exact:.8f} | {estimate:.8f} | {error:.2e} |"
    for spot, greek, exact, estimate, error in rows
)
display(Markdown("\n".join(table)))

The agreement is strong, but these are deliberately benign test points: one-year maturity, liquid-looking spots, and fixed bumps chosen for this scale. They confirm the formulas and finite-difference implementation are consistent here; they do not establish that the same bumps remain suitable across the surface.
From a validation perspective, the difficult region is short maturity and close to the strike. Gamma is then estimated from the small residual of three similar PVs. A wide spot bump smooths across the peak; a very narrow bump exposes floating-point cancellation. Vega has the analogous problem when the volatility bump produces a PV change close to numerical precision. A pointwise pass at \(T=1\) can therefore coexist with poor numerical Greeks in the part of the surface where risk is most concentrated.
For a put on the same stock, put–call parity gives \(\Delta_{\text{put}}=\Delta_{\text{call}}-1\); gamma and vega are the same under this model. The risk-shape discussion therefore carries across without duplicating the plots.
The next test is a bump-size sweep at one week around \(S=K\): where does truncation error give way to cancellation, and how should the bump scale with the width of the gamma peak?

title: Hosting WordPress with Amazon Lightsail
text:
NoteHistorical tutorial



Originally published in May 2020. Screenshots, prices, console navigation, and Bitnami paths describe the setup at that time and have not been checked against the current service. In this article, “VPN” is an old wording error: the steps concern a virtual server instance.



Some programming hobby. Let’s attempt to build a wordpress website using Amazon Lightsail. This is an easy tutorial and we should be able to build it in less than 10 minutes.

Sign Up for Amazon AWS
First of course, head over to Amazon AWS and sign yourself up! You’ll be prompted to give a credit card, but if used right the charges should be minimal. After that, you’ll be prompted with the AWS management console. On the “find services” tab, put in “Amazon Lightsail”. You’ll be shown the lightsail page.



Creating a wordpress instance
To create a VPN instannce, just click on “create an instance”, then choose an instance location (usually it is default to whichever closest to your current location). Select “linux/unix” platform, and select a blueprint “wordpress”. In this case the VPN will be pre-installed with Linux and Bitnami version of wordpress.

Scroll further downwards and you’ll be presented with choices, such as launch script or SSH key pairs. You’ll be fine not doing any of them for now. Also you can choose your instance plan. For starter, let’s use the cheapest $3.5 plan. It’ll generally work for websites with low volumes. Finally click on “create instance”.


Assign a static address
Next, we’ll need to assign a static address to the VPN instance. It’s free of charge, as long as you keep the VPN server up and running. To do that, go to the “lightsail” page, then choose “networking”. Next click on “create static IP”. Remember to attach the IP to the VPN instance you’ve just created. Oh yes, remember the IP address!



Get admin password and login
We’re not there yet! Now you’ll need to login into the wordpress. To do that, you’ll need a user/password. The fastest way to get your password is via SSH connection to your VPN server. To do that, go back to the lightsail page, on your VPN instance, click on the SSH button. The remote SSH session should start. Now type in the following
cat bitnami_application_password

Your user will be “user” with the password displayed. To login, just go to your wordpress using the static IP address previously, and click on the login button on the lower right corner.


Connecting a domain name to the host.
No one will connect to your website via an IP address (well, try memorizing it). Anyway, I assume you have a domain bought. To redirect the domain to your static IP address, just add an “A record” with host “@” and value being the static IP address.
After that, you’ll need to also configure wordpress to redirect to the right domain name. To do that, connect to your VPN’s SSH session, then go to
/opt/bitnami/apps/wordpress/htdocs/wp-config.php
And change the field “define(‘WP_SITEURL’) and (‘WP_HOME’)” to your domain name. You’re done!

title: Modelling COVID-19 Using an SEIR Model
text:
WarningHistorical notebook: parameter inconsistency



This is an unreviewed 2020 modelling experiment, preserved with its original code and charts. It is not a forecast. For the equations shown, the basic reproduction number near a fully susceptible state is \(R_0=\beta/\gamma\), giving \(\beta=R_0\gamma\). The original text and code below instead use division by \(\gamma\) when setting \(\beta\). Consequently, the charts do not represent the stated \(R_0=3.9\). They have not been regenerated, and the original conclusions should be read in that context. The date follows the original article metadata (20 March); the old filename used 29 March.



This notebook is my first attempt to use the compartmental models in epidemiology. This work is inspired largely by recent outbreak in COVID-19 and this article. This model is merely a draft and should not be used for projection!
The SEIR model is a model used to model infectious disease. The name itself is an acronym for Susceptible, Exposed, Infected, Recovered. When a virus is introduced to a population, an infected person may move from one location to another (also known as from one compartment to another compartment). This movement will move the virus throughout the population. The full model is as below, for S being fraction of population being susceptible, E being exposed, I for infected, and R for recovered.
\[
\begin{align}
\frac{dS}{dt} &= -\beta SI \\
\frac{dE}{dt} &= \beta SI - \alpha E \\
\frac{dI}{dt} &= \alpha E - \gamma I \\
\frac{dR}{dt} &= \gamma I
\end{align}
\]
There are 3 factors in these Odinary Differential Equations, which we will investigate them one by one.

\(\alpha\) is the inverse of incubation time. From recent researches, we can estimate the incubation time for COVID-19 to be 5 days.
\(\beta\) on the other hand is the average contact rate in the population. It is given by \(\beta = \frac{R_0}{\gamma}\), where \(R_0\) is the basic reproduction number of the disease. For COVID-19, the virus is estimated to have an \(R_0\) of around 1.4 - 3.9. For this simulation let’s take 3.9.
\(\gamma\) is the inverse of mean infection period. This is a tough to estimate parameter and we’ll be using 0.5, as suggested by other researches.

To build the simulation, let’s first define a function that solves the ODEs. The ODEs can be easily solved using Euler’s method. With these in mind, we define the function “RunSIER”.
#Start by importing tools
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
#we first build the model using forward Euler's method.
def RunSIER(state0, params, t):
    S0, E0, I0, R0 = state0
    S, E, I, R = [S0], [E0], [I0], [R0]
    alpha, beta, gamma = params
    dt = t[1] - t[0]
    
    #loop through the computation, using Euler's method to solve ODE
    #this is quick, but waste computation power by moving the arrays over & over again
    for _ in t[1:]:
        nextS = S[-1] - (beta * S[-1] * I[-1]) * dt
        nextE = E[-1] + (beta * S[-1] * I[-1] - alpha * E[-1]) * dt
        nextI = I[-1] + (alpha * E[-1] - gamma * I[-1]) * dt
        nextR = R[-1] + (gamma * I[-1]) * dt
        S.append(nextS)
        E.append(nextE)
        I.append(nextI)
        R.append(nextR)
        
    #return results
    return np.stack([S, E, I, R]).T
Now with the function in place, let’s try to simulate the model with default parameters we have choosen.
#define simulation parm
t_max = 100
dt = 0.01

#define initial state
t = np.linspace(0, t_max, int(t_max/dt) + 1) #each timestep is...
N = 1000 #number of people in population
state0 = 1 - 1/N, 1/N, 0, 0 #Susceptible, Exposed, Infected, Recovered. Initially, 1 exposed, others susceptible, no recoveries. Normalized

#define growth factors / parameters
alpha = 0.2 #alpha = 1/(incubation time). E.g. 5 days
gamma = 1.0/ 2.0 #gamma = 1/(mean infectious period)
beta = 3.9 / gamma #beta = infectious rate. R0 = beta/gamma (R0 is the "basic reproduction number"). Assume R0 = 3.9; 

#run simulation
params = alpha, beta, gamma
results = RunSIER(state0, params, t)

#and finally graphing the result
fig = plt.figure()
ax = plt.axes()
ax.plot(t, results);



png


From the simulation, it seems the entire population (100%) will be infected, leaving no susceptible compartments (see blue line). The rate of peak infection is at around 15d, with 60% compartments are exposed and 20% infection rate.
It’s obvious that with no intervention whatsoever, the coronavirus will spread throughout the entire population. Currently (25 Mar 2020), there are lots of cities that had went into social distancing or lock down orders. The chief idea is to retard the virus’s spread, and thus reducing the number of exposed & infected patient. From a modelling standpoint, it is interesting to understand the impact of social distancing. In SEIR model, the social distancing measure will impact the infectious rate, \(\beta\). To see how it’s impacted, let us half the infectious rate by adding a new factor, \(\delta\) = 0.5.
#define growth factors / parameters
alpha = 1.0 / 5.0
gamma = 1.0/ 2.0 
beta = 3.9 / gamma *0.5 #the infectious rate is halved to see the impact of social distancing

#run simulation
params = alpha, beta, gamma
results2 = RunSIER(state0, params, t)

#plotting graph
fig = plt.figure()
ax = plt.axes()
ax.plot(t, results2);



png


It seems that the virus is still potent enough to infect the entire population. However, the peak infection rate had reduced and shifted slightly to the right side. This shift of peak infection rate will buy our healthcare system some time, and avoid overcrowding the healthcare system. This is what everyone been talking about when they wanted to “flatten the curve”.
To visualize the flattening of curve further, we run several simulations and superimpose the graphs together.
#define growth factors / parameters
alpha = 1.0 / 5.0
gamma = 1.0/ 2.0
beta = 3.9 / gamma * 0.25

#run simulation
params = alpha, beta, gamma
results3 = RunSIER(state0, params, t)

#plotting graph
fig = plt.figure()
ax = plt.axes()
ax.plot(t, results[:,2],label='$\delta=1.0$')
ax.plot(t, results2[:,2],label='$\delta=0.5$')
ax.plot(t, results3[:,2],label='$\delta=0.25$')
plt.title('Plot of infected number, I against time')
ax.legend();



png


From the SEIR model without any social distancing measure, it seems that everyone in the population will be infected. However, with social distancing measure, the virus couldn’t infect everyone. This can be seen in the graph of susceptible population against time, where it flatlines at > 0 percent of population.
beta = 3.9 / gamma * 0.2
params = alpha, beta, gamma
results2 = RunSIER(state0, params, t)

beta = 3.9 / gamma * 0.1
params = alpha, beta, gamma
results3 = RunSIER(state0, params, t)

#plotting graph
fig = plt.figure()
ax = plt.axes()
ax.plot(t, results[:,0],label='$\delta=1.0$')
ax.plot(t, results2[:,0],label='$\delta=0.2$')
ax.plot(t, results3[:,0],label='$\delta=0.1$')
plt.title('Plot of Susceptible number, S against time')
ax.legend();



png


With stringent social distancing, it is likely that the \(\delta\) factor can be lower, which severely retards the virus’s spread.

title: The Option Gamma–Theta Relationship
text:
Black–Scholes option traders often discuss the gamma–theta relationship. For a delta-hedged option, it helps explain the relationship between time decay and exposure to spot moves. To derive it, consider the Black–Scholes PDE.
\[
\begin{align}
\frac{\partial V}{\partial t} + rS \frac{\partial V}{\partial S} + \frac{1}{2} \sigma^2 S^2 \frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial S^2}&= rV
\end{align}
\]
Now let’s put in the usual symbol for sensitivities,
\[
\begin{align}
\theta + rS\Delta + \frac{1}{2} \sigma^2 S^2 \gamma &= rV \\
\theta + \frac{1}{2} \sigma^2 S^2 \gamma &= r [V-S\Delta]
\end{align}
\]
The right-hand side is the financing term. Delta hedging does not make the option’s own \(\Delta\) or \(V\) zero: a hedge of \(-\Delta\) shares produces a portfolio with value \(V-S\Delta\).
When the financing term \(r(V-S\Delta)\) is negligible, for example in the zero-rate limit, the PDE gives the approximation
\[
\theta + \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2 S^2\gamma \approx 0.
\]
This relates calendar theta to the local curvature exposure. It does not imply that a delta-hedged position is riskless: realised spot moves, hedge frequency, and the model assumptions still matter.
The math can go slightly further. See Link. However this formula is a useful estimation for the theta-gamma breakeven for an delta hedged option. Finally, just to build an intuition on this relationship, we read from Hull’s book:

When gamma is positive, theta tends to be negative. The portfolio declines in value if there is no change in S, but increases in value if there is a large positive or negative change in S. When gamma is negative, theta tends to be positive and the reverse is true: the portfolio increases in value if there is no change in S but decreases in value if there is a large positive or negative change in S. As the absolute value of gamma increases, the sensitivity of the value of the portfolio to S increases.

For a broader visual treatment, see European Call Greeks: A Visual Risk Map.

title: Bootstrapping a SOFR Curve with QuantLib
text:
NoteFrom the previous website



Originally published in 2023. Code and figures are preserved as a historical example. The input workbook, SOFR.xlsx, is not present in this collection, so the code is shown without execution. The calibration results reported below have not been independently reproduced during migration.



I have been a valuation quant for the past 10 years. I have used numerous tools, especially C# and Python when it comes to modelling. However, we had always built codes from scratch, module by module.
This is the first time after years of hearing QuantLib that I decided to learn how to use them. They are surprisingly similar to how I would imagine an object-oriented derivative valuation module should look like. In this first exploratory post, I will try to bootstrap a SOFR swap curve (Bloomberg S490) and reprice the indices. Also, I am adopting the “just-publish-it” mindset for now. I will just publish anything with minimal verification - ping me if I have missed anything!
#Start by importing quantlib
import QuantLib as ql
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

#loading curve data from Excel
curveData = pd.read_excel("SOFR.xlsx")
systemDate = ql.Date(30,8,2023)
ql.Settings.instance().evaluationDate = systemDate

myIndex = ql.Sofr()
myCalendar = ql.UnitedStates(1)
myDayCount = ql.Actual360()
mySettlementDays = 2
#Here we use OISRateHelper to build a PiecewiseLinearZero curve. 
#Notice that OISRateHelper take in (SettlementDays,Period,Quote,Index)

ois_helpers = [ql.OISRateHelper(mySettlementDays,ql.Period(tenor),ql.QuoteHandle(ql.SimpleQuote(rate/100)),myIndex) 
               for rate,tenor in list(curveData[["MarketQuote","Tenor"]].itertuples(index=False))]
sofr_curve = ql.PiecewiseLinearZero(systemDate,ois_helpers,myDayCount)
sofr_curve.enableExtrapolation()

#sofr_curve.nodes() supposedly show the zero rates of the curve, however I am unable to verify it as of now.
print(sofr_curve.nodes())
#Now I attempt to reprice the OIS swaps
valuation_curve = ql.YieldTermStructureHandle(sofr_curve)
myIndex2 = ql.Sofr(valuation_curve)
swap_engine = ql.DiscountingSwapEngine(valuation_curve)
effective_date = myCalendar.advance(systemDate,mySettlementDays,ql.Days)

ois_swaps = []
for rate, tenor in list(curveData[["MarketQuote","Tenor"]].itertuples(index=False)):
    schedule = ql.MakeSchedule(effective_date,myCalendar.advance(effective_date,ql.Period(tenor)), #effective date, termination date
                            ql.Period("1Y"),calendar=myCalendar) #fixed rate frequency, calendar
    fixedRate = rate/100
    temp_oisswap = ql.MakeOIS(ql.Period(tenor),myIndex2,fixedRate,nominal=10000000)
    temp_oisswap.setPricingEngine(swap_engine)
    ois_swaps.append(temp_oisswap)
    
#we reprint the NPV of each swaps, expecting zeros
for a in ois_swaps:
    print(a.NPV())
